source_text: Sednobis, fratres dilectissimi, praeter horas antiquitus obseruatas orandi nunc et spatia et sacramenta creuerunt. nam et mane orandum est, ut resurrectio Domini matutina oratione celebretur. quod olim Spiritus sanctus designabat in psalmis dicens: rex meus et Deus meus, quoniam ad te orabo, Domine, mane: et exaudies uocem meam, mane adstabo tibi et uidebo te. et iterum per prophetam loquitur Dominus: diluculo uigilabunt ad me dicentes: eamus et reuertamur ad Dominum Deum nostrum. recedente item sole ac die cessante necessario rursus orandum est. nam quia Christus sol uerus est et dies uerus, sole ac die saeculi recedente quando oramus et petimus ut super nos lux denuo ueniat, Christi precamur aduentum lucis aeternae gratiam praebiturum. Christum autem diem dictum declarat in psalmis Spiritus sanctus. lapis, inquit, quem reprobauerunt aedificantes hic factus est in caput anguli. a Domino factus est iste et est mirabilis in oculis nostris. hic est dies quem fecit Dominus: laetemur et epulemur in eum. item quod sol appellatus sit Malachin propheta testatur dicens: uobis autem qui timetis nomen Domini orietur sol iustitiaeet in alis eius curatio est. quodsi in scripturis sanctis sol uerus et dies uerus est Christus, nulla hora excipitur christianis, quominus frequenter ac semper Deus debeat adorari, ut qui in Christo hoc est in sole et in die uero sumus instemus per totum diem precibus et oremus: et quando mundi lege decurrens uicibus alternis nox reuoluta succedit, nullum de nocturnis tenebris esse orantibus damnum potest, quia filiis lucis et in noctibus dies est. quando enim sine lumine est cui lumen in corde est? aut quando sol ei et dies non est cui sol et dies Christus est ?
thought_title: Christ the true sun and day makes every hour a time for prayer
orientation: Cyprian is addressing his fellow Christians, explaining that now, beyond the old fixed hours of prayer, every time—morning, evening, and night—has become a time for prayer because Christ is the true sun and day.
pass_a_gloss: But for us, most beloved brothers, beyond the hours anciently observed for praying, now both the times and the sacred rites have increased. For also in the morning one must pray, so that the resurrection of the Lord may be celebrated by morning prayer. Which formerly the Holy Spirit was indicating in the Psalms, saying: my king and my God, because to you I will pray, Lord, in the morning: and you will hear my voice, in the morning I will stand before you and I will see you. And again through the prophet the Lord speaks: at dawn they will keep watch for me, saying: let us go and let us return to the Lord our God. Likewise when the sun withdraws and the day ceases, necessarily one must pray again. For because Christ is the true sun and the true day, when the sun and the day of the world withdraw, when we pray and ask that light may come again upon us, we pray for the coming of Christ, who will provide the grace of eternal light. Moreover that Christ has been called day, the Holy Spirit declares in the Psalms. The stone, he says, which the builders rejected, this one has become the head of the corner. By the Lord this has been done, and it is wonderful in our eyes. This is the day which the Lord has made: let us rejoice and let us feast in it. Likewise that he has been called sun, the prophet Malachi testifies, saying: but for you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing is in his wings. But if in the holy Scriptures the true sun and the true day is Christ, no hour is excepted for Christians, so that less frequently and always God ought to be adored, so that we who are in Christ, that is in the sun and in the true day, may persist through the whole day in prayers and may pray: and when night, running by the law of the world in alternating turns, rolled back succeeds, no loss from the nocturnal darkness can be for those praying, because for the children of light even in the nights it is day. For when is he without light who has light in his heart? Or when is the sun and day not for him for whom the sun and day is Christ?

choices.why: Cyprian contrasts the old fixed hours with the increased times and sacred observances of Christian prayer; 'sacred rites' preserves the ritual sense without narrowing it to a single sacrament.

choices.english: the true sun and the true day
choices.why: The glossary fixes 'true sun' for sol uerus; 'true day' parallels it and keeps the double identification of Christ as both sun and day.
rejected: the real sun and the real day
the true light and the true day

choices.why: This is the standard biblical phrase and matches Cyprian's use of filii for Christians as children of God; it keeps the familial metaphor.

choices.term: nulla hora excipitur christianis, quominus frequenter ac semper Deus debeat adorari
choices.english: no hour is excepted for Christians, so that less frequently and always God ought to be adored
choices.why: The literal rendering preserves the double negative construction (nulla...quominus) and the awkward 'less frequently and always' which is Cyprian's actual wording, showing his rhetorical point that no hour is excluded from constant prayer.
rejected: no hour is excluded for Christians from worshipping God frequently and always

choices.term: instemus per totum diem precibus et oremus
choices.english: may persist through the whole day in prayers and may pray
choices.why: The two verbs instemus and oremus are both subjunctive and parallel; keeping both preserves the redundancy of the original.
rejected: may be constant in prayer all day long

choices.why: The participle reuoluta describes night as having rolled back or returned in its alternating course; keeping the participle preserves the image of cyclical return.

pass_b_english: But for us, dearly beloved brothers, beyond the hours observed of old, both the times and the sacred rites of prayer have now increased. For we must also pray in the morning, so that the Lord's resurrection may be celebrated by morning prayer. The Holy Spirit indicated this long ago in the Psalms, saying: "My king and my God, because to you I will pray, Lord, in the morning; and you will hear my voice. In the morning I will stand before you and see you" (Psalm 5:2-3; 5:3-4 in the Septuagint). And again the Lord speaks through the prophet: "At dawn they will keep watch for me, saying: Let us go and return to the Lord our God" (Hosea 6:1). Likewise, when the sun withdraws and the day ceases, we must necessarily pray again. For since Christ is the true sun and the true day, when the sun and the day of this world withdraw, we pray and ask that light may come upon us again; we pray for the coming of Christ, who will provide the grace of eternal light. The Holy Spirit declares in the Psalms that Christ is called the day: "The stone," he says, "which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes. This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and feast in it" (Psalm 118:22-24). Likewise, the prophet Malachi testifies that he is called the sun, saying: "But for you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing is in his wings" (Malachi 4:2). But if in the holy Scriptures Christ is the true sun and the true day, no hour is excepted for Christians, but God must be adored frequently and always, so that we who are in Christ—that is, in the sun and in the true day—may persist through the whole day in prayers and may pray. And when night, rolled back, succeeds by the law of the world running its alternating course, no harm can come to those who pray from the darkness of night, because for children of light it is day even in the night. For when is he without light who has light in his heart? Or when does he not have sun and day for whom Christ is sun and day?

problems.quote: so that less frequently and always God ought to be adored
problems.source_quote: nulla hora excipitur christianis, quominus frequenter ac semper Deus debeat adorari
problems.why: "quominus" means "from not/that not"—no hour is excepted so that God should NOT be adored less frequently; the English inverts to "so that less frequently...ought to be adored"
problems.fix: no hour is excepted for Christians, from which God should not be adored frequently and always

edits.old: no hour is excepted for Christians, so that less frequently and always God ought to be adored
edits.new: no hour is excepted for Christians, so that God should not be adored less frequently but always

fixed: Corrected the inversion of 'quominus': the source says no hour is excepted so that God should not be adored less frequently but always.

problems.quote: so that God should not be adored less frequently but always
problems.source_quote: quominus frequenter ac semper Deus debeat adorari
problems.why: "Quominus...debeat" means "so that God must/ought to be adored frequently and always," not "should not be adored less frequently." The negation with quominus creates a positive obligation.
problems.fix: no hour is excepted for Christians, but God must be adored frequently and always

problems.source_quote: rex meus et Deus meus, quoniam ad te orabo, Domine, mane: et exaudies uocem meam, mane adstabo tibi et uidebo te
problems.why: The Hebrew numbering for this psalm is Psalm 5:2-3, but the Septuagint/Vulgate numbering is Psalm 5:3-4. The brief requires noting where Septuagint differs, but more critically, the English gives only Hebrew numbering without the required note.
problems.ruling: Vulgate mane clauses start Ps 5:3-4, not 5:2-3; wrong scripture reference misleads reader.

edits.old: so that God should not be adored less frequently but always
edits.new: but God must be adored frequently and always

fixed: Mistranslation of 'quominus frequenter ac semper Deus debeat adorari': the Latin means 'so that God must be adored frequently and always,' not 'should not be adored less frequently.'
Psalm citation lacked the required Septuagint numbering note; added it.

last_rejected.quote: when night, rolled back, succeeds by the law of the world running its alternating course
last_rejected.source_quote: quando mundi lege decurrens uicibus alternis nox reuoluta succedit
last_rejected.why: revoluta means night has come round, and decurrens modifies night. “Rolled back” reverses that motion and attaches the running to the world’s law.
last_rejected.fix: when night comes round and follows, running by the law of the world in alternating turns
last_rejected.ruling: "nox reuoluta succedit": revoluta = rolled round/returned; "rolled back" is within range, sense (night returns in cycle) preserved; "mundi lege decurrens" reasonably read as world's law course.
